Adversary Emulation & XDR Detection Engineering

Detection Engineering  ·  Sophos XDR  ·  Atomic Red Team  ·  MITRE ATT&CK T1112

Ran an Atomic Red Team test against an endpoint on a default Sophos XDR configuration, ran roughly five tests until one registry persistence technique generated no detection, and wrote a custom rule that catches it.

CategoryHome Lab
StatusCompleted
PlatformSophos XDR · Windows 11
TechniqueT1112 Modify Registry
Purple Team Sophos XDR Atomic Red Team Detection Engineering Data Lake Search Registry Persistence MITRE ATT&CK Home Lab
Overview

A security product's default settings only show what the vendor decided to alert on. The only way to know what an environment would actually catch is to run known attacker behavior against it and see what happens.

This project followed that purple team loop on a single endpoint. Atomic Red Team simulated an ATT&CK technique (red), Sophos XDR was checked for a detection (blue), and the gap between the two was closed with a custom detection rule that was then validated by running the same test again.

Objectives
  • Run a series of Atomic Red Team tests against an endpoint protected by a default Sophos XDR configuration
  • Determine which techniques the default configuration detects and find one it does not
  • If it does not, confirm whether the telemetry exists, so the problem is a detection gap and not a visibility gap
  • Write a custom detection rule mapped to the technique and verify that it fires
Tools & Environment
  • Sophos XDR: endpoint agent plus the Security Operations console (Detections, Data Lake Search, Customization Rules)
  • Atomic Red Team ↗: library of small, ATT&CK-mapped tests run with the Invoke-AtomicTest PowerShell module
  • VirtualBox: hypervisor hosting the Windows 11 test endpoint, so the simulated attacks run in an isolated VM
  • Windows 11 endpoint: test host (Win-11-Defender) running the Sophos sensor
Walkthrough

Prerequisite: Install Atomic Red Team

Atomic Red Team runs through the Invoke-AtomicRedTeam PowerShell module. One command installs the execution framework and, with -getAtomics, downloads the library of test definitions to C:\AtomicRedTeam, the path seen in the test output below.

powershell: install Invoke-AtomicRedTeam
# Elevated PowerShell on the test endpoint
IEX (IWR 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redcanaryco/invoke-atomicredteam/master/install-atomicredteam.ps1' -UseBasicParsing);
Install-AtomicRedTeam -getAtomics

# Load the module in each new session
Import-Module invoke-atomicredteam

Setup notes: the Atomic Red Team documentation recommends excluding C:\AtomicRedTeam from antivirus scanning so the test definitions are not quarantined. If script execution is blocked, start PowerShell with powershell -exec bypass. Only run these tests on a machine you are willing to test on, such as an isolated VM, because they perform real attacker actions.

Step 1: Run the Atomic Test

The technique was not picked in advance. Roughly five Atomic tests were run, covering T1218.011 (Rundll32), T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder), and several T1112 (Modify Registry) tests. The default configuration detected every one until T1112 test 89, "Abusing MyComputer Disk Backup Path for Persistence", which went through unnoticed. That test is the focus of the rest of the project. It uses reg.exe to overwrite the BackupPath value under HKLM\...\Explorer\MyComputer so that a program of the attacker's choosing runs when Windows kicks off the backup activity. The test finished with exit code 0, so the registry change was made.

powershell: run the atomic
# Elevated PowerShell on the Windows 11 endpoint
Invoke-AtomicTest T1112 -TestNumbers 89

Atomic test T1112-89 executing successfully on the endpoint.

Step 2: Check for Detections

With the default configuration, the Sophos Detections queue was checked for open detections. It showed 0 detections. A technique that modifies a persistence-related registry value ran to completion and nothing was raised.

Detections queue after the test: no detections.

Step 3: Confirm the Telemetry Exists

No alert could mean the sensor never saw the activity, or that it saw it and had no rule for it. The two need different fixes, so a Data Lake query was run to tell them apart, searching process events whose command line contains backup.

sophos data lake: process events
FROM process WHERE commandline contains 'backup'

The query returned 17 process events, a cmd.exe and reg.exe pair for each test run, including the reg add against the MyComputer BackupPath key. The data was there.

Data Lake Search results: the sensor recorded every run.

Opening one event confirmed the full command line, the parent process (cmd.exe spawning reg.exe), the user, and the host. The event was labeled Not Blocked with no detection attached.

Event detail: command line, parent process, and user are all captured.

Finding: unlike the other tests, this was a detection gap, not a visibility gap. The sensor logged the behavior in full. The default configuration just had no logic that turned it into an alert.

Step 4: Study the Technique

Before writing logic, the Atomic's own definition was read to see exactly what the test does. It runs reg add on the MyComputer BackupPath key with REG_EXPAND_SZ data pointing at notepad.exe, and its cleanup command restores the value to sdclt.exe, the Windows backup utility. That gives two reliable anchors for a rule: the key name and the command used to write it.

The Atomic Red Team definition for the test, including its cleanup command.

Step 5: Write the Custom Detection Rule

A custom rule was created under Customization Rules, mapped to T1112, and set to High severity.

The first attempt was to build the rule on the registry / API schema, which would match the registry write itself regardless of which tool made it. That approach did not work: for reasons that were not determined, no data was being ingested for those schemas, so there was nothing for a rule to match. The rule was rebuilt on the process schema instead. Process events are the data that was confirmed to exist in Step 3. Because a process rule cannot see the registry change directly, the rule is made conditional on the typical commands used to establish this persistence: it matches process events whose command line references the MyComputer BackupPath key and contains a verb that writes to the registry. Requiring both keeps it from firing on every mention of the key and focuses it on modification.

sophos custom rule: Abusing MyComputer Disk Backup Path for Persistence
from process where commandline contains 'MyComputer'
  and commandline contains 'BackupPath'
  and (commandline contains ' add '
    or commandline contains 'Set-ItemProperty'
    or commandline contains 'New-ItemProperty'
    or commandline contains 'New-Item'
    or commandline contains 'SetValue')

The write verbs cover more than the Atomic's reg add. The same persistence could be set with PowerShell cmdlets or .NET calls, so those are included.

The custom rule in Sophos: query, MITRE tag, severity, and description.

Step 6: Re-run and Validate

The atomic was run again. This time the Detections queue showed the custom rule firing: "Abusing MyComputer Disk Backup Path for Persistence", with a threat score of 6.0, created seconds after the event. The queue lists the same detection twice, a repeat of one detection and not two separate findings.

Same test, new result: the custom rule now raises detections.

Results & Findings
0 → 1
Detections for the same test

Key finding: a default XDR configuration silently missed a registry persistence technique even though the data to catch it was already being collected. Testing it directly exposed the gap, and a small custom rule closed it.

Lessons Learned
  • Test your detections, don't assume them: a quiet console after an attack simulation is a result worth investigating, not a sign that things are fine
  • Separate visibility gaps from detection gaps: a Data Lake search for the raw events shows whether the fix is better telemetry or a new rule
  • Read the test before writing the rule: the Atomic's definition and cleanup command show exactly which strings and values to anchor on
  • Check which schemas actually have data: no data was being ingested for the registry / API schema, so a rule written against it could never fire. Falling back to the process schema meant writing the logic around the commands an attacker would actually run
  • Anchor on behavior and add context: pairing the key name with a write verb keeps the rule specific, and covering several write methods keeps it from being trivially bypassed
  • Map rules to ATT&CK: tagging the rule T1112 makes coverage easy to track against the framework
  • Validate by repeating the test: a rule only counts once the same simulation triggers it
